clue.text: Callas initially given divine voice, but little craft?

indicators.note: initially asks for only the opening letter of the word Callas

parts.note: an oracle was the voice through which a god spoke, as at Delphi

explanation.surface: Maria Callas sings like a goddess, yet the question ends on a tiny boat.
explanation.walkthrough: Callas looks like the famous soprano whose 'divine voice' completes the picture, but only her initial C is used.
explanation.definitionFit: A coracle is a small round wicker boat, so a little craft in the nautical sense.

clue.text: Cold, with sore throat

parts.note: C is the standard abbreviation for cold, as on taps
raw skin or a raw throat is sore and inflamed

explanation.surface: Someone complains of a chill accompanied by a painful throat.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'sore throat' together, but 'throat' is the definition and 'sore' gives RAW.
explanation.definitionFit: The craw is the crop of a bird, and loosely the gullet or throat of a person.

clue.text: Unusual combination of destructive and constructive forces

parts.note: the Royal Artillery, abbreviated RA, is the British army's destructive force of guns
the Royal Engineers, abbreviated RE, are the army corps that build bridges and works

explanation.surface: A physics lesson about rare balances of forces that tear down and build up.
explanation.walkthrough: The forces are British army units: the Royal Artillery (RA) destroys and the Royal Engineers (RE) construct; 'combination of' joins them.
explanation.definitionFit: Rare means seldom found or occurring, a plain synonym for unusual.

clue.text: Drive a camping convertible

indicators.note: something convertible can be changed into another form, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: An instruction to take a camper van with a folding roof out for a spin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Convertible' looks like a car to drive, but it signals that the letters of A CAMPING are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A drive is an organised campaign, as in a fundraising or recruitment drive.

clue.text: Irene ruined the bondsman

indicators.note: ruined means wrecked, so the letters of the name Irene are broken up and reset

explanation.surface: A woman named Irene brings disaster on a man who stood bail.
explanation.walkthrough: ERNIE is the machine that picks winning Premium Bonds, the UK government savings bonds that pay prizes instead of interest.
explanation.definitionFit: Ernie (Electronic Random Number Indicator Equipment) draws the Premium Bond prizes, a man of bonds in a playful sense.

clue.text: She turns in first-class stuff

indicators.note: turns means the run of letters is read in the opposite direction, right to left

parts.note: A1 means first-class, written here with the figure 1 as letter I
to cram is to stuff or pack tightly

explanation.surface: A woman hands in excellent material.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turns' reverses the whole of AI plus CRAM, giving MARC then IA; 'in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Marcia is a woman's name, so 'She' stands for any female name in crosswords.

clue.text: Bert meets Pope going round ancient city

parts.note: Bert is short for Albert, which also shortens to Al

indicators.note: going round means the letters of Pope turn about and come out in a new order

explanation.surface: A man called Bert has an audience with the Pope on a tour.
explanation.walkthrough: Bert and Al are both short for Albert, so one name stands for the other. The letters of POPE are then reshuffled to EPPO.
explanation.definitionFit: Aleppo in Syria is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world.

clue.text: Length of time in the middle

indicators.note: in places the word for time inside the word for the middle

parts.note: the centre is the middle point of something
taken as written

explanation.surface: A phrase about the stretch of time spent in the middle of something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Length of time' looks like one phrase, but 'Length' alone is the definition and 'of' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A centimetre is a unit of length, one hundredth of a metre.

clue.text: Star signs?

parts.note: read not as signs of the zodiac but as the signatures a celebrity writes for fans

explanation.surface: A question about the signs of the zodiac.
explanation.definitionFit: A star (a celebrity) signs autographs, so these are literally the signatures stars sign.

clue.text: Bitterness shown by army CO in trouble

indicators.note: trouble stirs things up, so the letters of army, CO and in are disturbed

explanation.surface: Resentment surfaces when an army's commanding officer gets into difficulty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in trouble' reads as one phrase, but 'in' is part of the fodder: ARMY CO IN gives the eight letters needed.
explanation.definitionFit: Acrimony is harsh bitterness of feeling or speech, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Sort of butter made from vegetable and fruit

parts.note: a pea is a green vegetable
botanically a nut is a hard dry fruit

explanation.surface: A recipe question about a spread blended from produce.
explanation.walkthrough: 'made from' is a link. A nut counts as a fruit botanically, which makes this charade fair.
explanation.definitionFit: Peanut butter is a spread made from ground peanuts, so this is a sort of butter.

clue.text: Call in church to fall on one's knees?

indicators.note: in puts the word for call inside the word for church

parts.note: CE is the Church of England
to ring someone is to call them on the phone

explanation.surface: A summons to worship leads people to kneel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to' is a link. The question mark admits that cringing, cowering in fear, is only loosely falling on one's knees.
explanation.definitionFit: To cringe is to cower or bow down servilely, pictured here as dropping to one's knees.

clue.text: Celebrity parachuting in attempt to impress

definitions.meaning: a famous name let fall, read literally as a well-known person dropped from the sky
casually mentioning famous acquaintances to make oneself seem important

explanation.surface: A famous person jumps from a plane to show off.
explanation.definitionFit: Name-dropping is mentioning famous people as if they were friends, a bid to impress; literally it is dropping a name.

clue.text: Lead, say, in hard rock

definitions.meaning: lead is an example of a dense metal of high atomic weight
a loud aggressive genre of rock music

explanation.surface: Lead singer performing in a hard rock band.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' is a link between the two senses. 'say' marks lead as one example of the class.
explanation.definitionFit: Heavy metals are dense ones like lead, and heavy metal is also a loud hard-rock music genre.

clue.text: It indicates the Naval Reserve officer is cold

parts.note: someone very cold turns blue
an ensign is a junior commissioned officer

explanation.surface: A remark that a Naval Reserve officer is chilly.
explanation.walkthrough: The charade runs in answer order, colour first. 'is' is a link. An ensign is also a flag, which is the definition's sense.
explanation.definitionFit: The Blue Ensign is the flag flown by Royal Naval Reserve ships, so it marks the Naval Reserve.

clue.text: Cracking up during a speech

parts.note: read as praising someone highly in a formal tribute, not as breaking down mid-speech

explanation.surface: A speaker loses composure while addressing an audience.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cracking up' suggests breaking down or laughing, but here it means talking up, praising.
explanation.definitionFit: To eulogise is to praise warmly, often in a formal speech, which is what cracking someone up means.

clue.text: Military band?

parts.note: read not as a group of army musicians but as a strip of braid sewn on a uniform sleeve

explanation.surface: A question about an army marching band.
explanation.definitionFit: A stripe is a band of braid on a uniform marking rank, so literally a military band.

clue.text: Time to bend an ear

indicators.note: to bend is to twist out of shape, so the letters of ear are rearranged

explanation.surface: An invitation to stop and listen for a moment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bend an ear' is an idiom for listening, but 'bend' here twists the letters of EAR; 'to' and 'an' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: An era is a long period of time, such as the Victorian era.

clue.text: Is one a complete swine to go this?

definitions.text: Is one a complete swine to go this?

parts.words: Is one a complete swine to go this?
parts.note: read as asking whether a whole pig behaves badly, though it means going all the way

explanation.surface: A question about whether someone is a total pig.
explanation.walkthrough: To go the whole way, without limits, is an idiom built on a complete pig; the swine is the literal sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Going the entire pig means doing something thoroughly, and literally names a complete swine.

clue.text: Contend it's a quarter past six

indicators.note: past places the quarter after six in the order of letters

parts.note: VI is six in Roman numerals
E for east is one of the four compass points, a quarter of the compass

explanation.surface: A claim about the time on a clock, quarter past six.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a time on a clock, but 'a quarter' is a compass point, E, and 'it's' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To vie is to compete or struggle against rivals, which is what contend means.

clue.text: Doesn't it have a service charge?

definitions.text: Doesn't it have a service charge?

parts.words: Doesn't it have a service charge?
parts.note: read as a restaurant bill query, but the service is worship and free means costing nothing

explanation.surface: A diner asks whether the bill includes a tip.
explanation.walkthrough: Free churches are Protestant churches independent of the state, such as Methodists; the joke takes 'free' as no charge.
explanation.definitionFit: A church holds services, and a free one would charge nothing, punning on nonconformist churches.

clue.text: Don't follow suit

parts.note: read as the card-game rule broken by playing another suit while holding one led

explanation.surface: Advice not to copy what others do.
explanation.walkthrough: In card games such as bridge, failing to follow suit when able is a breach of the rules with its own name.
explanation.definitionFit: To revoke at cards is to fail to follow suit when one could, the exact meaning here.

clue.text: Grown in the garden — not to scale?

definitions.text: Grown in the garden — not to scale?

parts.words: Grown in the garden — not to scale?
parts.note: read as a garden plant that a primate finds impossible to climb, a playful sense of scale

explanation.surface: A garden plan apparently drawn without proper proportions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not to scale' suggests a drawing; it means the tree baffles a climbing animal because its spiky branches cannot be climbed.
explanation.definitionFit: The monkey puzzle is a spiky garden tree said to be one that would baffle a climbing monkey.

clue.text: Menagerie's toilets, say, for Africans?

indicators.note: say signals that the words are to be spoken and heard rather than read

parts.note: a menagerie is a zoo and loos are toilets, so these are zoo loos

explanation.surface: An odd query about the lavatories in a collection of animals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for' is a link. LOO is everyday British for toilet. The question mark covers the soundalike.
explanation.definitionFit: The Zulus are a Bantu people of southern Africa, so they are Africans.

clue.text: Left-wing movement

definitions.meaning: short for a Trotskyist, a far-left political activist
a horse's gait between walk and canter

explanation.surface: A remark about a radical political movement.
explanation.definitionFit: A Trot is slang for a Trotskyist on the left, and a trot is also a pace or movement.

clue.text: Looked over carefully? I'd say!

indicators.note: say signals that the clue's I'd is spoken, giving a word that sounds the same

parts.note: the contraction of I would, taken as written

explanation.surface: A dry exclamation about scrutinising something closely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I'd say!' reads as an exclamation of agreement, but 'say' is the soundalike signal for I'd.
explanation.definitionFit: To eye something is to look at it closely, so eyed means looked over carefully.

clue.text: Follow an alternative man of the cloth

parts.note: to tail someone is to follow them secretly
or introduces an alternative, as in this or that

explanation.surface: An invitation to follow another clergyman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'man of the cloth' usually means a clergyman; here it is literal, a man who works with cloth.
explanation.definitionFit: A tailor makes clothes from cloth, so he is literally a man of the cloth.

clue.text: Lasting worry can be the very devil

parts.note: something old has lasted a long time
to harry is to harass or worry persistently

explanation.surface: Ongoing anxiety can be devilishly troublesome.
explanation.walkthrough: 'can be' is a link. OLD HARRY is an old English nickname for the Devil.
explanation.definitionFit: Old Harry is a traditional British nickname for Satan, so it names the very devil.

clue.text: Surgeon's paperknife?

parts.note: a surgeon's cutting blade that is also the name of a famous medical journal

explanation.surface: A question about a knife a surgeon uses to open letters.
explanation.walkthrough: The Lancet is a leading British medical journal, so the word is both a surgeon's paper and a surgeon's knife.
explanation.definitionFit: A lancet is a small surgical knife, and The Lancet is a medical paper read by surgeons.

clue.text: Saw about the digs?

parts.note: read as a question about lodgings, but it means spotted, sounding like placed at an excavation site

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether you saw anything about the lodgings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'digs' is British slang for lodgings; here it also suggests an archaeological dig, and the answer sounds like 'sited'.
explanation.definitionFit: Sighted means saw or caught sight of, and it sounds like being located at a site.
